doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 9, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: How drumset teaching and method books have changed
summary: Butch contrasts the few books of the late 1950s with today's manuals by Chapin, Latham, Cameron and Thigpen, and the rise of linear drumming.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Like you know you start playing and than you hear silence and then it starts to like sort of learn how to handle it. But it’s not a great way to do things. I guess it’s the best we have at this moment and we hope it will pass. I had a not a really formed question, but, with wind instruments and improvising, teaching jazz, the amount of material and research and so forth, jazz pedagogy has been leaps and bounds for years and years. I wonder if in the teaching of the drumset has been the same way. Has it changed a lot? Like the method books or what you’re expected to teach and what the students are expecting to learn?

It is changing quite a bit. It’s in the process right now, Monk, of changing a lot. When I first started learning all about drums and drumsets, there were just a couple of books that were my method of manuals that may teacher had supplied me and was giving me lessons out of. They didn’t go very far. They weren’t really adaptable to the drumset. But this is because I started taking lessons back in the late 50s, you know around 1957, ’58, and there wasn’t a whole lot of material. Things have changed and improved so much, you got away from a lot of the drum authors who were writing some pretty good “How To” books, but really couldn’t demonstrate very much, to the drummers who can play all over the place and imparting that knowledge and their own manuals, you’ve got the people © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

that, bless his heart, the great Jim Chapin. Or you have all other kinds of folks, one of the graduates from North Texas, one of the funkiest drummers in the world, Mr. Rick Latham, wrote an entire, a number of manuals about funk drumming. You’ve got brush work, Clayton Cameron, the great Clayton Cameron on brushes. You’ve got Ed Thigpen on brushes. You’ve got all sorts of wonderful manuals and drum methods now that are workable and usable, and they’re written by people who actually can play that. But it’s going into a different fashion now. There’s a whole other area of jazz that’s on the rise, along with the jazz/funk and the fusion and stuff for drummers anyway, it’s called linear drumming. And it’s where you have four-way coordination but not everything necessarily hits at the same time. You may have your hands and your feet all play but they don’t ever hit in conjunction with each other. It’s brilliant. It’s difficult. And it seems to be the coming thing. It’s just that with this pandemic I don’t know where we’re going to play it.
